newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Chirac may pay high price for gamble.
newsitem.headline: France's Chirac may pay high price for gamble.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac appears increasingly likely to pay a high price for his gamble of bringing forward a parliamentary election he did not have to hold until next March, analysts say.

Chirac, whose record of political judgment has been a mix of the inspired and the disastrous, has accumulated blunders since he dissolved parliament on April 21 and called a vote which the opposition left seems well placed to win next Sunday.
He called the snap poll in a bid to catch the opposition off guard and secure a solid centre-right majority for the remaining five years of his term.
But he seems to have utterly misjudged the depth of public discontent with his own broken promises on fighting unemployment and cutting taxes, according to opinion polls.
"The president should have been wary: when you give the people their say, they may end up having it," Le Monde publisher Jean-Marie Colombani said in an editorial.

The president's latest and most serious error may well have been to sacrifice his loyal if unpopular prime minister, Alain Juppe, without telling voters whom he would appoint in his place or what alternative policy he would pursue, analysts said.

"We already did not know what policy the RPR and the UDF had in this campaign, since they refused to run on their record, did not publish their plans and hid their intentions for the future. Now we don't even know who would conduct this unknown policy," Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin joked.

Had he waited until March 1998, the normal end of the legislature, Chirac might have been able to say that France had made the necessary efforts to qualify for a single European currency and the worst pain was now over.
With a bit of luck, he might have been able to point to economic growth returning and a slight dip in unemployment.

But diplomats who attended a NATO-Russia summit at Chirac's Elysee palace on Tuesday said presidential aides seem resigned to him having to share power with a Socialist-led government from next Monday, just two years into his term.

Analysing the results of last Sunday's first round, in which the combined left outpolled the coalition by more than four percentage points, while the extreme-right National Front won 15 percent, they said no single initiative could recapture the lost ground.

Some analysts had expected Chirac to give a clear indication in a television address on Tuesday night that he would appoint popular National Assembly president Philippe Seguin, a more socially-minded Gaullist, in Juppe's place.
"Probably Chirac's last chance to avoid defeat was if he had told voters 'I get the message and I'm going to appoint Seguin to pursue a more socially caring policy'," one analyst said.
"It might not have worked because at least it was worth a try," he said.

Instead, the president sought once again to reconcile the divergent forces within his coalition by promising both greater economic freedom and better social protection, both lower taxes and better public services.

Having called the election to seek a "new elan" to lead France into a single European currency, Chirac made no mention in his crucial speech either of the new elan or of European economic and monetary union.
Having thrown Juppe overboard as ballast, he took on the leadership of the coalition's campaign himself with an outright attack on "the socialist ideas of yesteryear".
That could weaken his presidency still further if voters force him to "cohabit" with a Socialist government.
Every gambit the president has tried in the campaign has either backfired or been neutralised by skilful opposition leadership by Jospin.

When Chirac published an article in provincial newspapers criticising the Socialists' record and ideas, few people read it and other media which had not been given the privilege of publishing the text were offended.

When he tried to use a visit by German Chancellor Helmut Kohl last week to warn voters that France would be weakened unless it spoke with a single voice in Europe, Jospin immediately replied that there was no reason why France should not speak with a single voice on EU issues.
He reminded voters that there had been no trouble on Europe between the late president Francois Mitterrand and the two right-wing governments with which he had shared power in 1986-88 and 1993-95.
Given the level of public disenchantment with the austerity policies required to qualify France for the single currency, the much-vaunted "Europe card" turned out to be a dud, not a joker.
